Lesson 1 · what a call actually costs

Every function call pushes a context

const app = 'rasmi'

function outer() {
  const user = 'ahmed'
  function inner() {
    const page = 2
    return [app, user, page]
  }
  return inner()
}
inner()page · [[Environment]] → outer
outer()user · [[Environment]] → global
globalapp · [[Environment]] → null
Per call: an environment record, plus a pointer to where the function was defined. That pointer is the scope chain — set at definition, not at call.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 1
04 / 41
Lesson 1 · proof, in six lines

Lexical, not dynamic

const label = 'module'

function read() { return label }

function caller() {
  const label = 'caller'
  return read()
}

caller()   // → 'module'
read was written next to the module-level label, so that is the one it sees — no matter who calls it, or from where.

Three consequences worth naming

  • A missing binding walks up, never sidewaysand ends in a ReferenceError, not undefined
  • let and const exist in the record from the first linebut reading before the declaration throws — that is the temporal dead zone, not "not hoisted"
  • var is initialised to undefined insteadwhich is why the two behave differently in a loop

Lesson 2 · the definition that survives an interview

A function plus the environment it was born in

function counter() {
  let n = 0                 // lives in counter's record
  return () => ++n           // holds a reference to it
}

const a = counter(), b = counter()
a(); a()   // 1, 2
b()        // 1  — a separate record
The frame popped; the environment record did not die, because the returned function still points at it.

The classic, and why it changed

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i))
// 3, 3, 3 — one binding, shared

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i))
// 0, 1, 2 — a fresh binding per iteration

Where you already rely on it

Three shapes, one mechanism

Private state

A value only the returned functions can reach. No #private, no convention, no way to poke at it from outside.

const store = makeStore()
store.get()  // ✓
store.state  // undefined

Remembered arguments

Every partial application, every curried handler, every onClick={() => remove(id)} in a list is a closure over id.

const on = (id) =>
  () => remove(id)

A slot between calls

The timer handle in debounce, the last-run stamp in throttle, the cache in memoize. Lesson 9 is three closures and nothing else.

let t
return (...args) => {
  clearTimeout(t); ...
}
If you can explain the counter on the last slide, you can already write debounce. Lesson 9 adds the timer, not the idea.

07 / 41
The other edge of the same knife

What the closure keeps alive

The cost

An environment record is reachable as long as any function that closes over it is reachable. One surviving callback can hold a 4MB response, a detached DOM node, or the whole component tree it was created in.

function attach(node) {
  const big = hugePayload()
  node.onclick = () => log('hi')
  // `big` is in the same record —
  // engines may keep it alive
}

The discipline

Keep the closed-over surface small: capture the one value you need, not the object it came from. Null out handles you own. Return an unsubscribe from anything that subscribes.

// capture the id, not the record
const { id } = job
return () => open(id)
"A memory leak is a closure that remembered something nobody asked it to." Lesson 8 measures exactly this.

Lesson 3 · read the call, not the definition

Four rules, checked in this order

function who() { return this }

who()                      // 1 · default
obj.who()                  // 2 · implicit
who.call(other)            // 3 · explicit
new Who()                  // 4 · construction
Arrows are not on this list: no this of their own, read from the enclosing scope. Bad methods, perfect callbacks.

The bug you have shipped at least once

A method passed by reference loses its dot

class Search {
  query = ''
  handle(e) { this.query = e.target.value }
}

const s = new Search()
input.addEventListener('input', s.handle)
// TypeError: Cannot set property of undefined
// the listener calls handle() — no dot, no this

Three fixes, in order of preference

  • Class field with an arrowhandle = (e) => { this.query = … } — bound at construction, one per instance
  • Wrap at the call siteel.addEventListener('input', e => s.handle(e)) — nothing to remember later
  • .bind(this) in the constructorworks, but you must remember the same reference to remove the listener
Never .bind() inline in a render — a new function identity every render breaks removal, memoisation and every equality check downstream.

Lesson 4 · delegation, without classes

Inheritance without classes or constructors

// Pure prototypal delegation
const protoUser = {
  login() { return `${this.name} logged in`; },
  hasAccess() { return this.role === 'admin'; }
};

// Create new object delegating to protoUser
const userA = Object.create(protoUser);
userA.name = 'Layla';
userA.role = 'editor';

console.log(userA.login()); // "Layla logged in"
console.log(userA.hasOwnProperty('login')); // false!
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(userA) === protoUser); // true

Differential Inheritance

userA only stores what makes it unique (name, role). All behavioral methods reside on protoUser.

The Prototype Pattern: new objects by delegating to an archetype, not by invoking a constructor.

Lesson 4 · what class is hiding

What 'class' is actually hiding

ES6 Class Syntax
class User {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  login() {
    return this.name;
  }
}
What V8 Actually Executes
function User(name) {
  this.name = name;
}
User.prototype.login = function() {
  return this.name;
};
// User is still a function!
console.log(typeof User); // 'function'
"Does JavaScript have true classes?" No — sugar over constructor functions and prototype chains. The runtime model is prototypal.

Lesson 4 · intercepting the object model

Intercept and control property access

A Proxy wraps a target object and intercepts operations using handler traps.
const user = { name: 'Omar', age: 28 };

const userProxy = new Proxy(user, {
  get(target, prop, receiver) {
    console.log(`Accessed ${String(prop)}`);
    return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver);
  },
  set(target, prop, value, receiver) {
    if (prop === 'age' && typeof value !== 'number') {
      throw new TypeError('Age must be a number');
    }
    return Reflect.set(target, prop, value, receiver);
  }
});

userProxy.age = 'thirty'; // throws TypeError!

The Core Traps

TrapTriggered By
getReading property (obj.prop)
setWriting property (obj.prop = v)
has'prop' in obj
deletePropertydelete obj.prop
applyCalling function (fn(...args))

Lesson 5 · before the first import

Which module system is this file?

// package.json — decides what .js means
{ "type": "module" }        // .js → ESM
// no "type", or "commonjs" → .js → CommonJS

// ESM project, a tool that wants CommonJS:
eslint.config.cjs           // .cjs wins

// JSON in ESM must say what it is
import config from './config.json'
  with { type: 'json' };
// CommonJS: require('./config.json')
FileWhat it is
.js .tsEither: "type" in package.json decides
.mjs .mtsAlways ESM; .mts → .mjs
.cjs .ctsAlways CommonJS; .cts → .cjs
.d.tsTypes only; runs nothing
.jsx .tsxJSX inside; the bundler compiles it
.vue .svelte .astroCompiled by a framework plugin
.wasm .nodeWebAssembly; native C++ addons
Need a guarantee whatever the project says? Use .mjs / .cjs, or .mts / .cts in TypeScript. .js and .ts follow "type".

Lesson 5 · at runtime

What 'import' actually does at runtime

// counter.js
export let count = 0;
export function inc() { count++; }

// app.js
import { count, inc } from './counter.js';

console.log(count); // 0
inc();
console.log(count); // 1 — live binding reflects update!
// count = 5; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

// CommonJS
const { count, inc } = require('./counter');
inc();
console.log(count); // 0 ← ما زالت 0! لأنها نسخة أُخذت لحظة الـ require

Three Phases of ESM Loading

  • ConstructionParse code into a Static Module Record and resolve dependencies
  • InstantiationAllocate memory locations for all exports & link bindings (no code runs yet!)
  • EvaluationExecute module code and fill the allocated memory slots with real values
CommonJS copies values; ESM links live bindings — which is why circular imports resolve there and half-build in CommonJS.

Lesson 5 · why that bites in tests

Why senior engineers call it an anti-pattern

1 · Test cross-pollution

Tests in one file share the module: B sees what A left.

import { cart } from './store';

test('A: adds an item', () => {
  cart.push('pen');
  expect(cart.length).toBe(1); // ✅
});

test('B: cart starts empty', () => {
  expect(cart.length).toBe(0); // ❌ got 1
});

2 · Hidden dependencies

The signature hides apiClient, so no mock can go in.

import { apiClient } from './apiClient';

function UserProfile() {
  const user = apiClient.getUser(); // hidden
  // …
}

// Explicit, and swappable for a mock
function UserProfile({ apiClient }) { … }
A reset in afterEach patches it. Passing it in fixes it.

Lesson 5 · why that bites on the server

One copy, every user

3 · The SSR request leak

A browser gives each user their own copy of the page. A Node or Next.js server loads the module once and serves every request from it.

// session.js — one copy for every request
let currentUser = null;
export function setUser(u) { currentUser = u; }
export function getUser() { return currentUser; }

// request A → setUser(A)
// request B → setUser(B)    same instant
// A's page  → getUser()  → B 😱

The fix · one copy per tree, per request

// React — each tree owns its state
function App() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);
  return (
    <CartContext value={{ cart, setCart }}>
      <Shop />
    </CartContext>
  );
}

// Server — build it inside the request
export async function handler(req) {
  const user = await getUserFromRequest(req);
  return render(user);
}
Module scope is shared by everyone and never resets. Nothing that belongs to one user or one request lives there.

Lesson 6 · before promises, inversion of control

A callback hands someone else your next step

// error-first callbacks, three steps deep
getUser(id, (err, user) => {
  if (err) return fail(err);
  getJobs(user, (err, jobs) => {
    if (err) return fail(err);
    getCompany(jobs[0], (err, company) => {
      if (err) return fail(err);
      render(user, jobs, company);
    });
  });
});

What you are trusting it to do

  • Call it exactly onceA promise settles once; a second resolve is ignored.
  • Never call it inline.then always runs later, on a microtask.
  • Hand you the errorA throw in any step becomes a rejection the next .catch sees.
Promises did not remove callbacks — .then still takes one. They turned the callback's unwritten contract into a guarantee.

20 / 41
new Promise · wrapping a callback API

Promisify once, await everywhere

// the executor runs synchronously, right now
function loadImage(src) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const img = new Image();
    img.onload = () => resolve(img);
    img.onerror = () => reject(new Error('load failed'));
    img.src = src;
  });
}

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
// ❌ wrapping what is already a promise
function getJobs() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    fetch('/api/jobs').then(resolve, reject);
  });
}

// ✅ just return it
const getJobs = () => fetch('/api/jobs');

// Node: util.promisify(fn) wraps any
// (err, value) callback API for you
resolve and reject are one-shot: the first call wins and every later call is ignored. That is the contract the callback never had.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 6
21 / 41
sleep at work · the same retry, written twice

Try three times, wait a second between

// 1 · callbacks only
function getJobsWithRetry(attempt, done) {
  fetch('/api/jobs')
    .then((res) => done(null, res))
    .catch((err) => {
      if (attempt >= 3) return done(err);
      setTimeout(() => {
        getJobsWithRetry(attempt + 1, done); // call itself again
      }, 1000);
    });
}

getJobsWithRetry(1, (err, res) => {
  if (err) console.log('failed');
  else console.log('ok');
});
// 2 · with sleep, which returns a promise
async function getJobsWithRetry() {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fetch('/api/jobs');
    } catch (err) {
      if (attempt === 3) throw err;
      await sleep(1000); // wait a second, then loop
    }
  }
}
Same requests, same timing. The promise adds no new power and no speed — only a different shape. The next slide is what that shape buys.

Usage · the difference shows up at the call site

The shape decides two things

1 · Who calls it

// callback: the caller is forced into callbacks too
getJobsWithRetry(1, (err, res) => {
  // everything that needs res lives in here
});

// promise: the result is a value like any other
const res = await getJobsWithRetry();
const [jobs, user] = await Promise.all([
  getJobsWithRetry(),
  getUser(),
]);

The gain is not inside the function. It shows up everywhere the function is used.

2 · The bug the callback hides

fetch('/api/jobs')
  .then((res) => done(null, res))
  .catch((err) => { /* retry */ });
  • The caller's code inside done throws.catch catches it, though the network was fine
  • It reads as a failed request and retriesfetch runs again, then done runs again
  • Success code runs two or three timesand the server gets every one of those requests
With async/await the result comes back once, and a throw in the caller's code stays with the caller — it never reaches the retry.

23 / 41
The same fetch, written three ways

await is a .then you can read top to bottom

// 1 · callbacks — one nesting level per step,
//     and an error check inside each one

// 2 · promises — flat, composable
getUser(id)
  .then(getJobs)
  .then(render)
  .catch(fail)
// 3 · async/await — the same chain
async function show(id) {
  try {
    const user = await getUser(id)
    const jobs = await getJobs(user)
    render(jobs)
  } catch (e) { fail(e) }
}
Dependent awaits belong in series. Independent ones cost both round trips for nothing — await Promise.all([getJobs(), getFilters()]).
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 6
24 / 41
Series or parallel · it is where the await goes

Two awaits in a row is a waterfall

// ❌ series: the second waits for no reason
const jobs = await getJobs();
const filters = await getFilters();

// ✅ parallel: start both, wait once
const [jobs, filters] = await Promise.all([
  getJobs(),
  getFilters(),
]);
// ❌ forEach ignores the promise you return
ids.forEach(async (id) => { await save(id); });
done(); // runs before a single save lands

// ✅ one at a time, in order
for (const id of ids) await save(id);

// ✅ all at once
await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => save(id)));
Start independent work together and await it once. Keep series only where the next call needs the last one's answer.

The four combinators, and when each is right

Pick by what failure should mean

Promise.allAll fulfil — or the first rejects
Promise.allSettledEvery promise finishes, whatever the outcome
Promise.raceThe first to settle, either way
Promise.anyThe first to fulfil; rejects only if all do
fast120ms · rejects
slow900ms · fulfils
middle500ms · fulfils
Pick a combinator, then run it.
Promise.all rejects on the first failure but cancels nothing — watch the other two keep going.

Lesson 7 · fetch, the rejection that never comes

A 500 is a successful request

// looks safe, ships a broken screen
async function loadJobs() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/jobs');
    // a 404 or a 500 still lands here
    const jobs = await res.json();
    // 404: the body is an HTML page → throws
    // 500: the body is { error: 'db down' }
    renderJobs(jobs);
    // → "jobs.map is not a function"
  } catch (err) {
    showError(err.message);
    // 404 → "Unexpected token '<'…"
    // the real cause never reaches here
  }
}
fetch()…
res.ok…
res.json()…
your code…
Pick a response, watch where it goes.
fetch rejects only on a network failure — DNS, offline, CORS, abort. Any HTTP status your server sends, 200 to 599, is a fulfilled promise.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 7

The fix · one wrapper, used everywhere

Turn every failure into a rejection, once

class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(status, url) {
    super(`${status} from ${url}`);
    this.name = 'HttpError';
    this.status = status;
  }
}

async function getJSON(url, opts) {
  const res = await fetch(url, opts); // network only
  if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res.status, url);
  if (res.status === 204) return null; // no body
  return res.json();
}
Now a 404 and a dropped connection arrive at the same catch, carrying enough information to tell them apart.
// the call site: one catch, every failure
try {
  renderJobs(await getJSON('/api/jobs', { signal }));
} catch (err) {
  if (err.name === 'AbortError') return; // ours
  if (err instanceof HttpError) showError(err.status);
  else showOffline();
}
fetch()…
if (!res.ok)…
204 · json()…
catch…
Pick a response, watch where it goes.

What a try can see

A try only catches what it awaits

// ❌ no await: the rejection skips the catch
try {
  save(form);
} catch (e) {
  toast(e); // never runs
}

// ❌ returned, not awaited: the same hole
async function load() {
  try { return fetchJobs(); }
  catch { return []; } // never runs
}
// ✅ await save(form); return await fetchJobs();
// ❌ thrown later, from another task
try {
  setTimeout(() => {
    throw new Error('boom');
  });
} catch (e) {
  // never runs: this try is long gone
}

// the smoke alarm for what nobody caught
addEventListener('unhandledrejection',
  (e) => report(e.reason));
No catch in the same async chain means an unhandled rejection: a console error in the browser, a crashed process in Node 15+.

29 / 41
AbortController · cancellation

Cancel what nobody is waiting for

const controller = new AbortController();

fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
  .then(render)
  .catch((e) => {
    if (e.name === 'AbortError') return; // ours
    showError(e);
  });

// the user typed again: drop the old request
controller.abort();
// React: cancel when the effect re-runs
useEffect(() => {
  const c = new AbortController();
  getJSON(url, { signal: c.signal })
    .then(setData)
    .catch(ignoreAbort);
  return () => c.abort();
}, [url]);

// a deadline, with no timer to clear
fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) });
// rejects with name 'TimeoutError'
An abort is not a failure. Catch AbortError and drop it; report everything else.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 7
30 / 41
Typed errors · cause · retry

Errors that know whether a retry helps

// would the same request work a moment later?
function retryable(e) {
  if (e.name === 'AbortError') return false; // we cancelled
  if (e instanceof HttpError) return e.status >= 500;
  return true; // the network dropped
}

async function withRetry(fn, tries = 3) {
  for (let i = 1; i <= tries; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === tries || !retryable(e)) throw e;
      await sleep(i * 300); // 300 ms, then 600 ms
    }
  }
}
// the call site keeps the real reason as cause
try {
  renderJobs(await withRetry(() => getJSON('/api/jobs')));
} catch (e) {
  throw new Error('Could not load jobs', { cause: e });
}
try 1
try 2
300 ms
try 3
600 ms
time →
Pick a server, watch the tries.
Retry network drops and 5xx, waiting longer each time. Never retry a 4xx or an abort, and keep the real error as cause.

31 / 41
Where to catch, and what to say

Three boundaries, three jobs

At the call

Only if you can do something: retry, fall back to cache, use a default. Never console.log and carry on.

At the feature

One boundary per screen. It owns the message the user sees and the retry button.

At the top

unhandledrejection feeds telemetry. A smoke alarm: anything here is a bug.

A 503: the call can do something about it……so it retries, and the user just sees jobs. Nothing above ever hears of it.A 404: no retry will fix it, so the call lets it go……to the screen's one boundary: an error message and a Retry button.A TypeError in a promise nobody awaited: no try can see it……until the top reports it. That is a bug to fix, not a message to show.
"A try only catches a throw in the same turn of the loop — so I await, wrap fetch so a status becomes a rejection, and give each feature one boundary."

Lesson 8 · what a leak actually is

Memory is freed when nothing can reach it

let user = { name: 'Sara', photo: bigImage }
user = null
// nothing points at that object any more → freed

const seen = []
function remember(u) { seen.push(u) }

remember({ name: 'Omar', photo: bigImage })
// still reachable through `seen` → never freed
Two objects, each reachable through a variable.user = null — the only arrow to Sara is gone.The collector starts from the roots……follows every arrow it finds……and marks everything it reaches.Nothing reached Sara: freed. Omar is kept.
A leak is not memory you lost. It is memory you can still reach — by accident, through something you forgot about.

33 / 41
Lesson 8 · the leak your single-page app has right now

A listener you never removed keeps everything it remembers

function openProfile(user) {
  const panel = document.createElement('div')
  panel.textContent = user.name
  document.body.append(panel)

  function onResize() {
    panel.style.width = innerWidth / 2 + 'px'
  }
  window.addEventListener('resize', onResize)

  return function closeProfile() {
    panel.remove()
    // ❌ forgot removeEventListener
  }
}
window is alive as long as the tab is open……its listener list holds onResize……onResize remembers panel and user……so the panel you removed is still reachable.One missing removeEventListener keeps the whole chain alive.
The page never reloads in a single-page app, so nothing wipes this for you. Open and close the profile fifty times: fifty panels, still alive.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 8
34 / 41
Lesson 8 · the fix

Every add needs a remove

Remove the same function

window.addEventListener('resize', onResize)

return function closeProfile() {
  panel.remove()
  window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize)
  // ✓ same reference → actually removed
}

Or one abort for all of them

const controller = new AbortController()
const { signal } = controller

window.addEventListener('resize', onResize, { signal })
window.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, { signal })

return function closeProfile() {
  panel.remove()
  controller.abort() // ✓ both listeners gone
}
Heap size while the profile opens and closes.Both versions grow on open and drop on close……but without the remove, each close keeps one panel. Twenty closes, twenty panels.
removeEventListener('resize', () => …) removes nothing — an arrow written twice is two different functions. Same rule for timers: every setInterval needs its clearInterval.

WeakMap: notes that disappear with the thing they describe

// Map holds its keys for ever
const notes = new Map()
notes.set(panel, { opened: Date.now() })
panel.remove()
// panel is off the page — but notes still holds it

// WeakMap lets its keys go
const notes = new WeakMap()
notes.set(panel, { opened: Date.now() })
panel.remove()
// nothing else holds panel → panel and its note are freed
Keeps its key aliveCan loop over it
Map / SetYesYes
WeakMap / WeakSetNoNo — that is the price
The page and the notes both point at panel. The WeakMap's arrow is dashed: it does not count.panel.remove() — the page lets go.The Map still holds it: kept. Nothing real holds it in the WeakMap: freed, note and all.
Use a WeakMap to attach extra data to an object you do not own — a DOM node, someone else's object. Use a Map when you own the data, and put a limit on its size.

Lesson 9 · utilities 1 and 2, one burst, two rules

debounce waits for quiet, throttle keeps a rate

debounce(fn, wait): every call resets the timer, and fn runs once, wait ms after the last call. throttle(fn, limit): the first call runs at once, then at most one per window.

events
debounce
throttle
Same events. Debounce waits for silence; throttle guarantees a rate.
Debounce: search-as-you-type, autosave, resize-settled, validating a field after typing stops.
Throttle: scroll position, mousemove, drag, analytics pings, infinite-scroll checks.

Lesson 9 · live coding, from an empty file

Both, in nine lines each

function debounce(fn, wait = 300) {
  let t                        // the closure slot
  function debounced(...args) {
    clearTimeout(t)
    t = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), wait)
  }
  debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(t)
  return debounced
}
Three details that get marked: ...args forwarded, fn.apply(this, …) so a method keeps its receiver, and a cancel for teardown.
function throttle(fn, limit = 300) {
  let last = 0, timer
  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now()
    const left = limit - (now - last)
    if (left <= 0) {
      last = now; fn.apply(this, args)      // leading
    } else if (!timer) {                   // trailing
      timer = setTimeout(() => {
        last = Date.now(); timer = null
        fn.apply(this, args)
      }, left)
    }
  }
}
Not an arrow at the top level: debounce(obj.method) would silently lose its receiver. Lesson 3, cashed in.

Lesson 9 · utility 3, a copy that shares nothing

deepClone(value)

function deepClone(value, seen = new WeakMap()) {
  if (value === null || typeof value !== 'object') return value
  if (value instanceof Date) return new Date(value.getTime())
  if (seen.has(value)) return seen.get(value) // cycle

  const copy = Array.isArray(value) ? [] : {}
  seen.set(value, copy)   // before the children
  for (const [key, entry] of Object.entries(value)) {
    copy[key] = deepClone(entry, seen)
  }
  return copy
}
filters holds an array and a Date. A primitive would simply be returned.{ ...filters } copies one level: the new object points at the same array and Date.copy.tags.push('vue'), and filters.tags changed too.Start again with deepClone: a new [], a new Date(…). Nothing shared.Each copy goes into seen before its children, so a cycle finds it there instead of recursing for ever.
In app code, structuredClone(value) already does this. The interview wants to see you write it — and name the four cases.

Lesson 9 · utility 4, subscribe and broadcast

EventEmitter

class EventEmitter {
  #listeners = new Map()   // event → Set of listeners

  on(event, fn) {
    const set = this.#listeners.get(event) ?? new Set()
    set.add(fn)
    this.#listeners.set(event, set)
    return () => this.off(event, fn)   // the unsubscribe
  }
  off(event, fn) {
    const set = this.#listeners.get(event)
    set?.delete(fn)
    if (set?.size === 0) this.#listeners.delete(event)
  }
  emit(event, payload) {
    const set = this.#listeners.get(event) ?? []
    for (const fn of [...set]) fn(payload)   // a copy
  }
}
Three on('saved', …) calls: one Set per event, so the same function can't be added twice.emit('saved', job) calls each one, looping over a copy: a listener added mid-emit waits for the next event.on returned an unsubscribe. B calls it and stops hearing. Every add needs a remove.A and C leave too. The last one out deletes the key, or the Map keeps an empty Set per event name for ever.
